title: 隣の家の人だけ  (Only the Neighbour Next Door)

segments.t: At ten o'clock Tuesday night at Hidamari Inn, Mio, Kenji, and Takashi hurry to the front door expecting an early city inspector—and find their next-door neighbour smiling on the step instead. Listen first.
ふう！心臓が中庭の木を飛び越えるかと思いましたよ！
手紙を届けてくれた、隣の本屋さんの店主だけでしたね！
渡された市役所のハンコ付きの封筒を読んでくれ、美央。
「地域の文化財カフェ審査……水曜日、午後三時ちょうど。」
ああ、よかった……今夜じゃありません！中の確認リストを読んでください、美央さん！
一つ目。通りのわかりやすい看板と、近所の人が入れる開いた中庭。
門には油を差したし、木の看板も塗った……よし、完了だ。
二つ目。明るくて安全な室内の席と、熱いお茶と作りたての食べ物。
椅子が十二脚、きれいな窓、新しい銅の電線……それに謎の白い壺が二つです！
誰かが寝る前に、今すぐその壺にラベルを貼れ、美央。
左のスプーンは……甘い！右のスプーンは……海みたいにしょっぱい！両方に大きな赤いラベルを貼ります！
危機一髪でした！皆さん、もう寝ましょう……朝の六時はすぐ来ますよ！
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
ふう！心臓が中庭の木を飛び越えるかと思いましたよ！

'Phew! I thought my heart was going to jump right over the courtyard tree!' That opening sigh is the exact sound you breathe out when a scare passes, and the Japanese word for 'heart' here means the physical organ pounding in your chest.
手紙を届けてくれた、隣の本屋さんの店主だけでしたね！
'It was only the bookshop owner next door bringing our mail!' Japanese builds friendly shop names by tacking 'shop' plus polite 'san' onto what they sell, turning 'book' straight into 'bookshop'.
渡された市役所のハンコ付きの封筒を読んでくれ、美央。
'Read the stamped city envelope she handed you, Mio.' Instead of the textbook polite 'please read', Kenji uses the blunt, warm request ending a veteran coworker uses with a trusted teammate.
「地域の文化財カフェ審査……水曜日、午後三時ちょうど。」

'"Local Heritage Cafe Review — Wednesday, three o'clock sharp."' The word at the very end, "choudo", means right on the mark—with clock times it gives 'three sharp', and at a cash register it means 'exact change'.
ああ、よかった……今夜じゃありません！中の確認リストを読んでください、美央さん！
'Thank goodness—not tonight! Please read the checklist inside, Mio!' Listen to Takashi's relief word:
よかった。
Literally 'it was good', which Japanese speakers reach for whenever English says 'thank goodness!' or 'what a relief!'.
一つ目。通りのわかりやすい看板と、近所の人が入れる開いた中庭。

'Item one: a clear street sign and an open courtyard where neighbours can enter.' Adding the word for 'eye' onto a number turns 'one' into 'the first' or 'item one', a clean way to start any spoken checklist.
門には油を差したし、木の看板も塗った……よし、完了だ。
'Gate oiled, wooden sign painted—all right, check.' Handyman Kenji ticks off his list with "yoshi", the crisp 'all right!' Japanese speakers say when a job looks solid.
二つ目。明るくて安全な室内の席と、熱いお茶と作りたての食べ物。

'Item two: bright, safe indoor seating with hot tea and freshly made food.' Adding "tate" onto 'make' builds 'freshly made'—swap in 'bake' and you get 'fresh out of the oven' on bakery signs on Japanese shopfronts.
椅子が十二脚、きれいな窓、新しい銅の電線……それに謎の白い壺が二つです！
'Twelve chairs, clean windows, new copper wire—and two mystery white jars!' Chairs in Japanese take a special counter built from the kanji for 'leg', because chairs and tables stand on legs.
誰かが寝る前に、今すぐその壺にラベルを貼れ、美央。
'Stick labels on those jars right now before anyone sleeps, Mio.' Kenji remembers the sugar-and-salt mix-up right on time, pairing 'now' with 'immediately' for 'right this second!'.
左のスプーンは……甘い！右のスプーンは……海みたいにしょっぱい！両方に大きな赤いラベルを貼ります！

'Left spoon... sweet! Right spoon... salty as the sea! I am putting big red labels on both!' Here you get two essential kitchen opposites in one breath—"amai" for sweet and "shoppai" for sharply salty.
危機一髪でした！皆さん、もう寝ましょう……朝の六時はすぐ来ますよ！

'Crisis averted! Everyone to bed—six in the morning comes fast!' The four-kanji idiom at the start literally pictures a crisis hanging by a single strand of hair—the classic Japanese phrase for a close call.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.
ふう！心臓が中庭の木を飛び越えるかと思いましたよ！

門には油を差したし、木の看板も塗った……よし、完了だ。

Sugar and salt are clearly labelled in red, the checklist is clear, and Wednesday morning's six-o'clock kitchen shift awaits. See you next time.
また明日！
